definitionEn: knowing a lot about modern technology.
existingExample: Tech-savvy children often teach their parents how to use new apps.

definitionEn: using the internet to hurt, threaten or embarrass someone.
existingExample: Schools need clear policies to tackle cyberbullying.

definitionEn: a disadvantage or problem.
existingExample: The main drawback of online shopping is that you cannot try products before buying them.

definitionEn: an innovation that transforms an industry or market.
meaningVi: công nghệ đột phá (làm thay đổi cả ngành)
existingExample: Streaming was a disruptive technology for the music industry.

definitionEn: using the latest technology.
existingExample: The laboratory is fitted with state-of-the-art equipment.

definitionEn: a type of AI in which computers learn from data.
existingExample: Machine learning helps banks detect fraudulent transactions.

definitionEn: extremely large data sets analysed to reveal patterns.
existingExample: Retailers use big data to predict consumers' buying habits.

definitionEn: storing and processing data on remote servers.
existingExample: Cloud computing allows small firms to avoid buying expensive servers.

definitionEn: the protection of computer systems from attack.
existingExample: Hospitals must strengthen their cybersecurity.

definitionEn: an incident in which private data is stolen or exposed.
existingExample: A data breach exposed millions of customers' personal details.

definitionEn: converting data into a code to keep it secure.
existingExample: End-to-end encryption protects private messages.

definitionEn: the record of a person's online activity.
existingExample: Teenagers should consider the digital footprint they leave online.

definitionEn: receiving more information than one can process.
existingExample: Constant notifications contribute to information overload.

definitionEn: the length of time someone can concentrate.
meaningVi: khả năng duy trì tập trung
existingExample: Some researchers believe short videos are shortening attention spans.

definitionEn: a period without using digital devices.
meaningVi: thời gian tạm ngừng thiết bị số
existingExample: A weekend digital detox can reduce stress.

definitionEn: a person who dislikes or fears new technology.
existingExample: Many older people describe themselves as technophobes.

definitionEn: someone who uses new technology as soon as it appears.
existingExample: Early adopters often pay high prices for new devices.

definitionEn: devices worn on the body, such as smartwatches.
existingExample: Wearable technology lets people monitor their heart rate.

definitionEn: a computer-generated three-dimensional environment.
existingExample: Virtual reality is used to train surgeons.

definitionEn: digital images layered onto the real world.
existingExample: Augmented reality apps let shoppers see furniture in their own homes.

definitionEn: making you feel completely surrounded by an experience.
existingExample: Museums now offer immersive digital exhibitions.

definitionEn: the way a person interacts with a computer or app.
existingExample: A clear user interface makes apps easier for older people.

definitionEn: easy to use without instructions.
existingExample: Tablets are intuitive enough for young children to use.

definitionEn: designing products to stop working or become outdated after a certain time.
existingExample: Critics accuse phone manufacturers of planned obsolescence.

definitionEn: progress in technology.
existingExample: Rapid technological advancement has transformed healthcare.

definitionEn: converting information into digital form.
existingExample: The digitisation of medical records saves doctors time.

definitionEn: the use of digital technology to change how organisations operate.
existingExample: Banks have undergone a rapid digital transformation.

definitionEn: buying and selling goods online.
existingExample: E-commerce has hit traditional high-street shops hard.

definitionEn: a society in which payments are made electronically.
existingExample: A cashless society may exclude elderly people.

definitionEn: a website or app that connects users or sellers.
existingExample: Online platforms allow small businesses to reach global customers.

definitionEn: a very large and powerful technology company.
meaningVi: tập đoàn công nghệ khổng lồ
existingExample: Governments are trying to regulate the power of tech giants.

definitionEn: complete control of a market by one company.
existingExample: Critics argue that some search engines hold a near monopoly.

definitionEn: to make a process operate by machine.
existingExample: Banks have automated many routine tasks.

definitionEn: the science of designing and using robots.
existingExample: Advances in robotics are transforming car factories.

definitionEn: an aircraft with no pilot, controlled remotely.
meaningVi: thiết bị bay không người lái
existingExample: Drones are used to deliver medicine to remote villages.

definitionEn: making solid objects by printing layers of material.
existingExample: 3D printing can produce custom medical implants.

definitionEn: technology that works with extremely small particles.
existingExample: Nanotechnology could make solar panels more efficient.

definitionEn: using physical features such as fingerprints for identification.
existingExample: Biometric passports store a digital image of the holder.

definitionEn: technology that identifies people from their faces.
existingExample: Facial recognition cameras raise serious privacy concerns.

definitionEn: software that responds to spoken commands.
existingExample: Voice assistants can help elderly people who live alone.

definitionEn: a computer program that simulates conversation.
meaningVi: chatbot, trợ lý trò chuyện tự động
existingExample: Many companies use chatbots to answer basic queries.

definitionEn: artificial intelligence that creates text, images or music.
existingExample: Generative AI raises difficult questions about copyright.

definitionEn: unfair outcomes produced by automated systems.
existingExample: Algorithmic bias can lead to unfair hiring decisions.

definitionEn: people checking and controlling automated decisions.
meaningVi: sự giám sát của con người
existingExample: Medical AI tools still require human oversight.

definitionEn: based on the analysis of data.
existingExample: Data-driven decisions reduce guesswork in business.

definitionEn: a situation with no clearly right moral choice.
meaningVi: tình thế khó xử về đạo đức
existingExample: Self-driving cars pose an ethical dilemma in unavoidable accidents.

definitionEn: being responsible for actions and willing to explain them.
existingExample: There is little accountability for harmful algorithms.

definitionEn: to develop faster than something else.
existingExample: Technology often outpaces the laws that govern it.

definitionEn: to change or progress as quickly as something else.
existingExample: Schools struggle to keep pace with technological change.

definitionEn: absolutely necessary.
existingExample: Smartphones have become indispensable for most people.

definitionEn: spreading widely through an area or group.
existingExample: Technology has a pervasive influence on daily life.

definitionEn: advanced and complex.
existingExample: Criminals use increasingly sophisticated scams.

definitionEn: a failure to work properly.
meaningVi: sự trục trặc; hoạt động sai
existingExample: A software malfunction grounded hundreds of flights.

definitionEn: the ability of devices or software to work together.
existingExample: Compatibility issues prevent some apps from running on older phones.

definitionEn: the amount of data that can be transmitted at once.
existingExample: Video calls require high bandwidth.

definitionEn: a high-speed internet connection.
existingExample: Many rural areas still lack high-speed broadband.

definitionEn: a person who grew up with digital technology.
meaningVi: người sinh ra trong thời đại số
existingExample: Digital natives adapt quickly to new applications.

definitionEn: a lack of contact with other people.
existingExample: Excessive gaming can lead to social isolation.

definitionEn: getting pleasure immediately without having to wait.
existingExample: Social media feeds a culture of instant gratification.

definitionEn: to do several things at the same time.
existingExample: Research suggests people multitask less effectively than they think.

definitionEn: able to use computers competently.
existingExample: Most office jobs require staff to be computer literate.

definitionEn: communication over a distance by telephone, internet, etc.
existingExample: Telecommunications have shrunk the distance between countries.

definitionEn: a device sent into space to orbit the earth.
existingExample: Satellite imagery helps scientists track deforestation.

definitionEn: a legal right to be the only one to make or sell an invention.
meaningVi: bằng sáng chế; cấp bằng sáng chế
existingExample: The company holds patents on its battery design.

definitionEn: ideas and inventions protected by law.
existingExample: Online piracy undermines intellectual property rights.

definitionEn: illegally copying software, films or music.
existingExample: Online piracy costs the creative industries a great deal of revenue.

definitionEn: software whose code anyone may use and modify freely.
existingExample: Many universities use open-source software to cut costs.

definitionEn: a first model of a new product.
existingExample: Engineers tested a prototype of the new battery.

definitionEn: learning by trying different methods until one works.
existingExample: Many inventions were developed through trial and error.

definitionEn: to start selling a product for profit.
existingExample: Universities often struggle to commercialise their research.

definitionEn: to make goods in large quantities.
existingExample: Cheap mass-produced goods have changed shopping habits.

definitionEn: never having happened before.
existingExample: Information now spreads at an unprecedented speed.

definitionEn: increasing more and more rapidly.
existingExample: Computing power has seen exponential growth.

definitionEn: options that control who can see your data.
existingExample: Users should review their privacy settings regularly.

definitionEn: being unidentified when using the internet.
existingExample: Online anonymity can encourage abusive behaviour.

definitionEn: the networks and systems that support digital services.
existingExample: Reliable digital infrastructure is vital for remote learning.

definitionEn: ideas or guesses about something without firm evidence.
existingExample: There has been much speculation about the future of work.

definitionEn: reliable information based on careful measurement.
existingExample: Policy decisions should be based on solid data rather than fear.

definitionEn: large in size, value or importance.
existingExample: The policy had a substantial impact on youth unemployment.

definitionEn: a person who expects bad things to happen.
existingExample: Pessimists argue that robots will take most jobs.

definitionEn: happening or existing in many places or among many people.
existingExample: Smartphone use is widespread among teenagers.

definitionEn: something that does not happen or exist very often.
existingExample: Jobs for life are now something of a rarity.

definitionEn: information that shows what a situation is like at one particular time.
meaningVi: bức tranh tại một thời điểm
existingExample: The census provides a snapshot of the population every ten years.

definitionEn: chosen by the participants themselves rather than at random, which may bias results.
meaningVi: tự chọn tham gia (không ngẫu nhiên)
existingExample: Online polls often rely on a self-selected sample.

definitionEn: to cause someone or something to be in a particular state.
existingExample: New technology may render some skills obsolete.

definitionEn: the series of steps by which you move to more senior jobs.
existingExample: Internships help graduates get onto the first rung of the career ladder.

definitionEn: The capability of distinct computer systems, platforms, or devices to exchange and interpret data seamlessly.
meaningVi: khả năng tương tác và liên thông giữa các hệ thống
existingExample: Mandating technical interoperability between competing messaging platforms prevents dominant firms from locking users inside closed ecosystems.

definitionEn: The time delay between initiating a digital instruction or data transmission and receiving the corresponding response.
meaningVi: độ trễ truyền dẫn tín hiệu hoặc phản hồi của hệ thống
existingExample: Ultra-low network latency is indispensable for remote robotic surgery, where even a split-second lag could endanger patients.

definitionEn: The capacity of a software architecture or technological system to handle growing workloads efficiently without performance loss.
meaningVi: khả năng mở rộng quy mô mà vẫn giữ hiệu năng
existingExample: Cloud-native infrastructures provide remarkable scalability, enabling public agencies to absorb sudden surges in online tax filings.

definitionEn: The mathematical science of encoding and decoding information to guarantee secure communication and verify authenticity.
meaningVi: mật mã học bảo mật thông tin số
existingExample: Advances in post-quantum cryptography are urgently needed to ensure banking networks remain impervious to next-generation decryption.

definitionEn: Distributed across multiple independent nodes rather than controlled by a single central authority or server.
meaningVi: phi tập trung, phân tán quyền kiểm soát trên nhiều nút mạng
existingExample: Proponents argue that decentralised digital registries reduce single points of failure and strengthen resilience against cyberattacks.

definitionEn: A cryptographically linked, distributed digital ledger that records transactions transparently across a peer-to-peer network.
meaningVi: công nghệ chuỗi khối lưu trữ sổ cái minh bạch bất biến
existingExample: Beyond cryptocurrency, supply-chain auditors are trialling blockchain to verify the ethical provenance of exported raw materials.

definitionEn: A computational machine-learning architecture composed of interconnected nodes modelled loosely on biological brain pathways.
meaningVi: mạng nơ-ron nhân tạo mô phỏng cơ chế học của não bộ
existingExample: Trained on millions of satellite photographs, the neural network detected illegal logging clearings with unprecedented accuracy.

definitionEn: Synthetic video, audio, or imagery generated by deep learning to convincingly depict events or speech that never occurred.
meaningVi: video/âm thanh giả mạo tinh vi tạo bằng AI
existingExample: Electoral regulators warn that a convincing deepfake released hours before polling day could severely distort voter trust.

definitionEn: Malicious software that encrypts an organisation's vital files and demands monetary payment to restore access.
meaningVi: mã độc tống tiền khóa dữ liệu hệ thống để đòi chuộc
existingExample: A coordinated ransomware intrusion forced several municipal hospitals to revert to paper records for nearly two weeks.

definitionEn: The fraudulent practice of sending deceptive electronic messages disguised as reputable institutions to steal credentials.
meaningVi: lừa đảo giả mạo nhằm đánh cắp thông tin nhạy cảm
existingExample: Even sophisticated corporate firewalls remain vulnerable when employees fall prey to highly personalised spear phishing campaigns.

definitionEn: Any software intentionally crafted to disrupt, damage, spy upon, or gain unauthorised control over computer systems.
meaningVi: phần mềm độc hại xâm nhập và phá hoại máy tính
existingExample: Routine software patching remains the single most cost-effective defence against intrusive malware targeting public infrastructure.

definitionEn: A previously unknown software security flaw that attackers can exploit before developers release a corrective patch.
meaningVi: lỗ hổng bảo mật mới phát hiện chưa có bản vá
existingExample: National cybersecurity agencies collaborate with ethical hackers to identify any zero-day vulnerability before hostile actors weaponise it.

definitionEn: Security verification that confirms an individual's identity using unique biological traits such as fingerprints or iris patterns.
meaningVi: xác thực danh tính bằng đặc điểm sinh trắc học
existingExample: While biometric authentication streamlines mobile banking logins, compromised physiological data cannot simply be reset like passwords.

definitionEn: A distributed computing paradigm that processes data close to the physical devices generating it rather than in distant data centres.
meaningVi: điện toán biên xử lý dữ liệu trực tiếp gần nguồn phát
existingExample: Autonomous factory robots rely on edge computing to analyse sensor feeds instantaneously without saturating central bandwidth.
